LiDAR-based systems are being increasingly used.  LidarSLAM, a Lidar-based system that combines simultaneous localization and mapping, is a critical underlying technology.  However, as systems become smaller and more power-efficient, they are also more susceptible to numerical errors due to miniaturized components and rigorous manufacturing processes.  These inaccuracies can significantly impact the performance of localization and mapping systems, leading to errors in maps and system trajectories.  Nonetheless, existing evaluations of LidarSLAM systems typically disregard these issues, largely due to the high processing requirements for processing full-scale real-world data.  To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel and efficient framework, called PointNet-based System Evaluation (PNS-Eval), that leverages the popular PointNet neural network to reduce data dimensions and accelerate processing times.  The framework accelerates processing times through optimized data reduction, comparative metrics, and a multi-dimensional assessment of errors, including map and trajectory errors.

The proposed system consists of a Cooper pair box (CB) linked to a single-electron transistor (SET) via an auxiliary island, with the drive and read gates integrated into the SET. in high-resolution day-glow spectra of planetary nebulae, focusing on Tc 1 and NGC 5546.  Observations revealed a non-negligible degree of asymmetry on certain day-glow lines, particularly those with higher ionic potentials.  Asymmetries are characterized using an Gaussian asymmetry model and quantified through an asymmetry parameter $\alpha$.  Asymmetry patterns are observed to vary with ionic potential, electron density, and whether the lines originate from the nebula's inner or outer regions.  Higher electron densities are found to correlate with increased day-glow line asymmetries, suggesting the influence of Stark effects.  Higher $\alpha$ values are indicative of stronger magnetic fields within the planetary nebulae.  Magnetic field estimates, derived from simulations and based on day-glow line data, are approximately $10\text{--}50\text{ G}$ in the nebula's gas flow, and about $1000\text{ G}$ at the photocentre.  Our study provides crucial groundwork for accurately interpreting high-resolution day-glow spectra and for studying the interaction between stars and their surrounding environment in planetary nebulae.

We propose defining tellable jokes as those that can be articulated in a single sentence, assuming the listener possesses general world knowledge.  
Although this definition seems intuitive, it's not clear whether it holds up under scrutiny.  
In this study, we assess the feasibility of this definition by attempting to paraphrase a set of just a few hundred jokes.  
To automate this process, we developed two methods to identify three aspects of a joke: its setup, its punchline, and the core idea that connects them.  
Our experimental results show that current language models struggle to grasp the definition of tellable jokes, as they can't effectively predict which jokes can be summarized.  
In contrast, our findings suggest that the more relatable definition of tellable jokes is comprehensible and potentially tapable using advanced techniques like combining world knowledge with large language models.

However, most existing OOD detection methods fail to account for the reality that in real-world applications, domains are rarely isolated, but rather interconnected through their data distributions.  In this research, we address the challenge of OOD detection in cases where samples from multiple domains are present during inference.  Our proposed approach, InterDomain Detection (InterDomainDet), effectively identifies both known OOD samples as well as entirely unknown domains.  The core idea of InterDomainDet is to model the distribution of all possible domains (including unknown ones) via a hierarchical Bayesian framework.  This model is designed to be highly flexible and can adapt to various domain characteristics, such as pixel-level variations and semantic differences.  Notably, InterDomainDet does not require any labeled training data.  By leveraging unsupervised domain adaptation, our method is capable of accurately capturing both domain-specific and general features.  In our experiments, we demonstrate that InterDomainDet outperforms current OOD detection techniques on single-domain and multi-domain OOD detection tasks.

is a set of edges that forms both a perfect matching and a cutting set.  It has been established in previous research that perfect matching cuts are highly prevalent in random graphs with a typical structure.  It has been demonstrated in sparse graphs that a perfect matching cut is present if the graph is sufficiently robust and planar in sections.  It is known that in dense graphs, a perfect matching cut is present if the graph is sufficiently robust and sectionally balanced in terms of edge distribution.  It is an open question whether a perfect matching cut is present in any graph with a typical structure, provided it contains a perfect matching.  In this paper, it is shown that a perfect matching cut is present in any graph with a robust, sparsely distributed structure that has the same minimum edge connectivity as any pair of nodes.  It is also shown that a perfect matching cut is present in any graph with a robust, evenly distributed structure that has the same minimum edge connectivity as any pair of nodes, plus an additional margin.  It is known that for graphs with a robust, sparsely distributed structure where the minimum edge connectivity is greater than the number of nodes divided by three, a perfect matching cut is present if and only if a perfect matching is present.

However, it is demonstrated that for any algorithm estimating a finite-dimensional parameter from arbitrarily long streams, even in the presence of noise, robustness is unattainable.  In particular, we identify two prominent cases where robustness is impossible: (1) estimating the median of arbitrarily long streams, and (2) estimating the mean of streams where the heavy-tailed distribution has a second moment, both with constant space.  In addition, our findings reveal that for estimating the median, robustness cannot be achieved even when the stream is non-adversarial, even with the allowance of a polynomial number of errors.  In contrast, a new algorithm is introduced for estimating the mean under these conditions, requiring only a nearly optimal space of $\tilde{O}(d^{1/3})$.  Our results have significant implications for a diverse range of streaming applications, notably those where data can be streamed only once.

To address this challenge, we investigate a specialized class of real-time processing systems known as frequency trading networks. These systems are designed to efficiently handle low-latency data and are characterized by their use of highly interconnected layers of asynchronous processing units. Unfortunately, the high interconnectivity and heterogeneous nature of these networks, combined with the requirement for real-time synchronization, pose significant challenges for distributed training methods. Frequency trading networks typically employ field-programmable gate array hardware, which is prone to stochastic failures, further complicating training. In this study, we introduce a novel algorithm that enables synchronized training of these networks in a distributed manner, and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments conducted on FPGA hardware.

These bursts, characterized by rapid movement of dislocations, are responsible for distinctive acoustic signatures known as the Portevin--Le Chatelier effect.  The deformation process is governed by a competition between deformation rates and the dynamics of stress-induced dislocation reactions within materials.  Recent advancements in experimental techniques have enabled the observation of individual reaction events in real-time using techniques like scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction. The theoretical framework is validated through comparison with experimental data and x-ray experiments on copper single crystals.

Challenge: Traditional methods often struggle with these issues, resulting in average-based predictions that fail to capture the object's precise boundaries.  Solution: In response, we introduce an approach that utilizes an object detection model paired with a boundary-aware loss function, which encourages each prediction to align more closely with the object's actual contours.  Methodology: Our proposed method redefines the object detection task to produce predictions that align with object boundaries rather than entire negative boxes.  Application: We demonstrate the effectiveness of our boundary-aware loss function in improving the performance of existing object detection models, particularly R-FCN and SSD. To address this issue, we present a collection of 1000 synthetic point sources that encompass the necessary information for such analyses. Neutrino masses and DM are both DoFs that could be linked through the so-called "neutrino DM portal" interactions. In this context, we explore a specific interaction between the DM and neutrinos, where both are linked to the Higgs triplet field. In this framework, both neutrino masses and DM self-interactions are induced. In this paper, we focus on the induced DM self-interactions, which are shown to have significant implications for DM structure formation. In this study, we derive the induced DM self-interaction cross section within the Higgs triplet model, and then apply it to the cosmic DM power spectrum and sub-halo abundance. Our results indicate that this model can be constrained by the lack of observed DM over-densities, leading to an allowed DM mass range of 10 GeV to 100 TeV. Furthermore, this model can potentially explain the observed sub-halo abundance, particularly for DM masses of 100 GeV to 10 TeV.

To address this challenge, this study proposes a control approach that incorporates a friction and stiffness observer along with a feedback linearization control method, all expressed in joint space. The system's dynamics were first simplified by considering the friction and stiffness parameters as constant, then the control strategy was adjusted to account for these parameters in the transformed, friction and stiffness-inclusive coordinates. Although magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has long been used to visualize brain lesions associated with MS, it has limitations in detecting subclinical inflammation and changes in cognitive function.  In contrast, electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive method for recording brain activity, correlating with cognitive function, but interpreting EEG data is complicated due to interindividual variability.  To overcome these challenges, we collected EEG data from 100 individuals with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) and 100 healthy controls (HC) while they performed an auditory oddball task.  Using EEGNet, a deep learning model, we extracted EEG features and classified the two groups with 91.5% accuracy, primarily driven by differences in cognitive processing within the frontal cortex.  Notably, individuals with CIS exhibited reduced P300 amplitudes in this area.  When applying the same model to distinguish between HC and patients with established MS, classification accuracy dropped to 72.5%, likely due to greater cognitive impairment in the latter group.  Our findings suggest that combining MRI and EEG data could provide a more comprehensive understanding of neurological functioning in CFS and CSM patients, ultimately contributing to more personalized clinical management.

growing interest in utilizing neural operators to resolve forward and inverse problems associated with partial differential equations.  Traditional neural network architectures, however, fail to adhere to specific constraints, such as data processing hierarchies and specific mathematical properties of solution operators.  To address this challenge, we propose the Water-filling Fourier Operator network (WIFO), a novel architecture that can be trained through backpropagation while conforming to these constraints.  Specifically, WIFO combines a neural function approximator with the principles of water-filling to allocate computational resources and maintain specific properties of the operator, such as surjectivity.  The proposed framework is demonstrated to be effective in a variety of scenarios, including learning the solution operator for the heat equation and the inverse of a positive function, outperforming conventional methods like the Fourier Neural Operator and standard multi-layer perceptrons.  The results of our study are made available to the research community through the release of both our code and trained models.

evolution of initially localized states during thermalization.  Focusing on states that evolve from local density matrices, we analyze how the range of entanglement grows over time.  Our theoretical framework combines a Heisenberg equation of motion with the condition of local purity, which is derived from comparing the evolving state to a thermal state.  Our findings show that in systems with low initial excitation, the entanglement growth rate is proportional to the initial local purity and the system's Hamiltonian's operator growth rate.  This relationship holds for states that evolve from local density matrices, regardless of their specific structure.  Our theoretical predictions are validated by comparing them to the expansion of entanglement entropy in initially localized states with unit chemical potential.  We also establish an upper limit on the entanglement growth rate in systems with local Hamiltonians, which is system-independent and relates to the maximum rate of operator growth in quantum systems.

This relationship, combined with a critical threshold, indicates a higher density of star formation in areas with greater density.  This finding suggests a universal connection between chemical composition and structure in major spiral galaxies, and supports the existence of a central bar in M33.  However, further study is needed to confirm this and further our understanding.

  this paper, we explore the possibilities and constraints of leveraging

  that a fast-slow learning system must meet: (1) the necessity of joint

  the development of algorithms capable of processing arbitrary functions,

  inference, and reinforcement learning - against these criteria, examining

  second criterion due to its inability to handle a broad range of scoring

  establishes supervised regression and reinforcement learning as prototype

background noise in gravitational wave detectors stems from scattered thermal radiation.  Analyzing the effect of spatially coherent and incoherent thermal photons on detector strain sensitivity, we discovered that in the high-frequency range above a few kilohertz, scattered thermal radiation behaves like a source of shot noise.  This thermal shot noise results from the random fluctuations in the number of absorbed photons and can be minimized by reducing the temperature of detector components and optimizing their material properties for minimal thermal conductivity and mean free path.  Notably, this limit may become comparable to quantum shot noise, which is already mitigated through squeezing techniques, by employing low-temperature scattered thermal radiation.  In contrast, we found that the effect of spatially incoherent thermal photons gives rise to frequency-dependent force noise, whose amplitude is significantly larger than thermal shot noise, particularly dominant in a specific regime centered on a few hundred hertz.  Overcoming this force noise at 250K and 10cm scale demands extremely low thermal conductivity and high photon mean free path values of $10^{-12}$ Watts per Kelvin, which may be achievable with advanced engineering.  In order to outperform the best current design of Advanced LIGO, scattered thermal radiation force noise needs to remain below $3.2\times10^{-10}$ Newtons per Kelvin at a frequency of 425 hz.  Addressing both thermal shot noise and incoherent force noise is crucial in designing future detectors

By combining the principles of extremal Reissner-Nordstr\"om black holes with plasmonic systems, we've identified parallels between their critical behaviors.  Specifically, both contain two distinct phase transitions, one of which is linked to the non-zero charge of these entities, while the other occurs at charge zero and is analogous to nearing the center of a black hole.  Notably, the occurrence of this second phase transition in plasmonic nanoparticles is influenced by their charge, while an extremal nanoparticle's charge reaches its maximum possible value, much like the charge-to-mass ratio of an extremal black hole.  While the concept of Hawking radiation from nanoparticles has been previously debated, our findings reveal that the extremal nanoparticle's behavior at zero charge is driven by spontaneous emission, while non-extremal particles can undergo a shift from states of overcharged stability to undercharged decay through spontaneous radiation, much like the process of radiation from extremal black holes.

To do this, we employ linear perturbation theory combined with numerical simulations. While solving the Euler-Lagrange PDE from the Brenier's theorem theoretically guarantees an optimal solution, it often fails to provide accurate results in practice due to the complex nature of the problem. This paper introduces a novel solver that achieves a significant improvement in computational efficiency by a factor of at least one order of magnitude. We prove that such systems consist of two distinct types: strings spread across light-like surfaces and point singularities located on timelike surfaces.  We identify the specific forms of these systems by utilizing the symmetry properties inherent to them.  We find that the latter class includes point singularities at the origin, known as the Taub metric, and additional 'hidden' singularities at the origin and two other points - $x^0 = \pm a$ - that are mutually at rest. By conducting direct numerical simulations, we examined the rebound of air bubbles and the rebound of water droplets above a non-wetting layer of varying thicknesses. The problem is redefined and solved for two scenarios: (1) when $\mathbf{P(x)}$ is symmetric and bounded degree, and (2) when $\mathbf{P(x)}$ has low dimension, regardless of its degree. This study presents a novel approach to model the collective dynamics of randomly distributed spherical particles in a viscous fluid using a stochastic lattice model.  By numerically simulating this model, we examine how the size distribution of particles affects their overall movement and separation from one another.  Our findings are compared to theoretical models and prior research, revealing key patterns in particle behavior across various scales.  Notably, we discovered that larger particles tend to migrate to the surface due to buoyancy, while smaller particles become trapped in viscous boundary layers, resulting in distinct zones of concentrated and sparse particle populations.  These observations are supported by theoretical models that account for the varying effects of drag and repulsion forces based on particle size.

the interstellar medium significantly impacts the dynamics of astrophysical plasmas.  However, measuring these fields poses a challenge due to fields below ~10 micron in size being invisible in optical polarimetry.  Although past studies using optical polarimetry have inferred estimates of total magnetic fields based on plasma pressure balance, the actual distribution of magnetic field sizes remains uncertain.  By analyzing synchrotron radiation from electrons that are diffusing through the interstellar medium, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the magnetic field's length scales.  A key factor in this process is the mean free path of diffusing photons, which is heavily influenced by the combined effects of dust scattering and the Mossbauer effect in neutral hydrogen atoms.  Our findings reveal that recent estimates of the mean free path of infrared photons may be overestimated, particularly at shorter wavelengths where our calculations suggest the mean free path is actually smaller by an order of magnitude.  Despite this correction, we predict that synchrotron radiation from electrons can escape into space only when they reach a minimum momentum of ~3 x 10^-2, which is less than previously estimated.  This implies that synchrotron radiation can effectively probe low energy electrons (~500 eV) in the interstellar medium.  A possible method for detecting these electrons involves using a space-based infrared spectrograph to observe bright sources like the full moon. ube technique is a widely-used approach in medical image segmentation.  Nevertheless, this method has significant shortcomings stemming from its reliance on integrating along specific paths.  These issues become particularly pronounced when tracking contours through complex regions, such as those with occlusions or abrupt intensity fluctuations.  To address this, we propose the Flow-based Method (FlowMethod) to circumvent common pitfalls associated with the tube method.  Our approach reimagines the level set function as the accumulation of flow between the source and the contour, which then allows us to employ established flow techniques, including divergence computation and vector field extension, to obtain a modified Allen-Cahn equation solvable via diffusion-based methods.  Our experiments across multiple imaging modalities, including MRI and CT, demonstrate the effectiveness of FlowMethod in brain segmentation tasks.

By applying a x-ray pump and an optical probe, our group has conducted a comprehensive study on a solitary sulfur atom embedded in a titanium dioxide substrate at a temperature of 300K.  The x-ray pump creates a highly charged sulfur hole in a 3p orbital, which then undergoes motion due to a "pushing" force resulting from the interaction with an optical field.  We were able to observe the migration of the sulfur hole towards an adjacent ${\rm O}_{2}$ molecule by examining the x-ray absorption spectra of the system.  Our findings demonstrate that within 2.5fs after the initial x-ray pulse, the oxygen atom begins to be oxidized by capturing a sulfur hole.  This research is a significant step forward in utilizing an x-ray pump in the field of solid-state research with XFELs.

deep learning, there's a considerable amount of research still needed to fully comprehend how these complex neural networks function.  This study delves into one of the key mysteries surrounding deep learning: 'hidden units saturation' - the phenomenon where many neural network units fail to activate during training and remain inactive.  Our analysis reveals that this issue is prevalent across a wide range of deep learning applications, posing a significant obstacle to achieving optimal performance.  Furthermore, our research provides empirical evidence that the 'pruning' of these inactive units is essentially an automatic process, which has profound implications for understanding the apparent efficiency of deep neural networks.  To address the problem of hidden units saturation, we've developed a novel approach called HiU-SAN - a simple yet effective method to ensure that all neural network units are fully utilized.  When applied to HiU-SAN, standard pruning techniques result in models with reduced latency and improved efficiency.  The HiU-SAN approach has been shown to yield notable gains in both classification and object detection tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art models on the CIFAR-100 and COCO benchmarks.

to exhibit novel magnetic and electronic properties that differ from those found in their bulk forms. This phenomenon, known as interface engineering, holds significant promise for developing novel devices that exploit these unique properties. To create such devices, a thorough understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing these interface phenomena is essential. This study utilizes a first-principles approach to investigate the characteristic properties of layered perovskite structures and their associated interfaces, focusing on a group of oxide systems that exhibit distinct magnetic and electronic states. These systems, consisting of nonmagnetic oxide layers and iron-based superconductor-like layers, demonstrate unique properties, including metal-insulator transitions and exchange interactions, that can be influenced by factors such as layer thickness and doping levels. This research uncovers the complex interplay between these layers and their interfaces, which exhibit unusual states, including polarized spin states and localized electrons, that exhibit similar characteristics to strongly correlated materials and unique quantum entanglement. This discovery paves the way for further exploration of layered structures and their interfaces, which could be used to study unique physical phenomena and develop novel oxide-based devices that exploit quantum entanglement.

visible light communication (VLC) are emerging as promising solutions to address the escalating demand for wireless data. Merging these technologies into a hybrid system offers a dual benefit of high data transmission rates and uninterrupted communication, albeit with a challenge of directional antennas requiring precise alignment. To address this challenge, we propose a novel cooperative hybrid access scheme in an Internet of Things (IoT) environment, enabling a base station to authenticate and enable devices without the need for exact antenna alignment. In this setup, VLC is used for high-rate data transmission, while mmWave is used for data transmission, with the VLC and mmWave antennas operating in a full-duplex mode. To mitigate self-interference, we model the relationship between the power of the interfering mmWave signal and the enabling VLC light, and employ a non-linear power amplifier model to reduce self-interference to negligible levels. To optimize the system, we develop a low-complexity, learning-based approach to maximize a weighted sum objective function that balances the data transmission rates of both technologies. Our results show that the proposed hybrid access scheme is feasible and can significantly reduce both types of interference while maximizing the system's performance.

Studies in this model have shown that characteristics like heterogeneity, clustering, and the "small-world" effect influence a network's ability to perform functions like information processing and adaptation. Previous research has demonstrated the "small-world" property in biological neural networks using electroencephalogram data and cat brain maps, as well as network "world-size" values around 2-3 times the logarithm of the network's node count in these cases. However, despite their importance, most models of information processing networks fail to consider the "small-world" parameter, and there is little information available on how this parameter impacts a network's ability to perform its intended functions. In this study, we introduce a method for calculating the "small-world" parameter and conduct computer simulations to analyze the effects of this parameter and the network's connectivity and heterogeneity on its performance. We created tasks for the network to process and adapt to, and found that as the "world-size" value decreases, the network's ability to perform these tasks improves, particularly in terms of learning new associations and adapting to changes in the environment. In our results, we observed "optimal performance" when the "small-world" value is within the range of 2-3, which we argue corresponds to the "optimal world-size" found in biological neural networks.

-level atom interacting with a single mode of an electromagnetic field exhibits rich dynamics, including dark states that result in a form of population damping known as coherent spontaneous emission. When the atom's dipole moment is treated classically, the mechanism of coherent spontaneous emission is explained by flux damping arising from the continuum of vacuum modes. This paper presents a Bayesian framework for developing turbulence models using machine learning from such extensive datasets.  The proposed approach treats models of turbulent phenomena as probabilistic entities and derives their underlying distributions from observed data using a learning algorithm.  This results in acquired models capable of not only providing predictions but also quantifying their associated uncertainties.  The general and flexible nature of the presented framework allows for the incorporation of various data sources, physical principles, and model structures.  Furthermore, the unified Bayesian formulation simplifies the comparison of competing models.  To illustrate the application of this approach, the paper includes the derivation of the Gaussian process regression and normalizing flow as well-known algorithms within the machine learning domain.  Although the benefits of uncertainty quantification in the meteorology field have been previously explored, there is a lack of widespread adoption of these methods in modeling complex systems characterized by turbulent behavior.  To address this gap, the manuscript is written with the intention of guiding machine learning experts and data scientists in applying their knowledge to this critical and underexplored domain.

The $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry has emerged as an intriguing concept that can lead to novel phenomena, such as non-Hermitian skin effects and exceptional points. Leveraging the $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry, we've developed a method to convert any given Hamiltonian into a form with symmetry, simply by adding a carefully designed decoupling term based on a few parameters. The approach utilizes the concept of unitary basis transformation to ensure universality, making it applicable to systems of any dimension with any degree of freedom, as long as they possess a two-site unitary basis. The unitary basis transformation ensures that the modified Hamiltonian retains information about the original system. As a result, we can observe the consequences of the unitary basis transformation, such as the preservation of non-Hermitian skin effects and exceptional points. The decoupling scheme is also versatile, allowing us to transform distinct topological phases into the same symmetry class. The methodology is further validated by proposing and experimentally confirming two models, including the Soni-Wan-Knittel-Hsieh-Zhang model and the Soni-Wan model.

model providers who wish to encourage researchers to utilize their models. Until now, there has been little research on incentivizing model users to refrain from stealing the provided model. This paper introduces the concept of defensive distillation and explores utilizing it as a defensive measure to protect the provider's model. Our proposed approach involves the provider training a defensive model that classifies the users' attacked model as the provided one, thus identifying any attacked model as different from the provided model. When the user's attacked model yields significantly lower accuracy than the provided model, it is classified as the provided one, effectively revealing the weakness of the user's attacked model. Our experiments on three datasets and multiple learning algorithms demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposed defensive measure in exposing the flaws of various types of model attacks.

probabilistic finite automata is an ongoing challenge in the field of automata theory.  It has been established that such automata can recognize exponentially complex functions under deterministic output, but the complexity class of NP contains functions computable by more complex, NP-class containing versions of these automata.  In this work, we present an NP-containing automaton that computes a pseudo-random bit generator based on the work of Adleman, which requires a significantly smaller and less powerful configuration.  Our specific automaton has a quadratic-sized structure,  $2\log^2 n$ states, and can be efficiently simulated by a deterministic algorithm with a one-time, exponentially complex preprocessing step.  As a direct consequence, we show that pseudo-random generators can exist without the need for circuits that are larger and more powerful than those in the P complexity class.  It is also important to note that this is the first instance of a pseudo-random generator being generated by an automaton whose complexity is not at least as high as a standard NP machine.  This discovery has significant implications for the relationship between the complexity of an automaton and the ability to generate pseudo-random numbers.  Specifically, it allows us to construct a random number generator based on a machine whose complexity is exponentially smaller and more manageable than previously thought.  This has a direct impact on the ability to create such generators with state and transition complexity that are within the NP and P complexity classes, respectively.

  The introduction of star-gauge spaces also enables the redefinition of essential analytical tools, including series, limits, sums, power series, differentiability, integrals, and differential equations. 
  The redefinition of these tools is further facilitated by the study of metric functions within the framework of star-gauge spaces. 
  The specific focus of the article is the redefinition of the Bessel functions of the first kind through the lens of continuity, differentiation, and integration within the framework of star-gauge spaces.

We demonstrate how this framework can address a range of cosmological and astrophysical challenges while maintaining compliance with dark matter detection efforts.  To counteract the "overproduction" of dark matter through the matter-matter mechanism, we suggest that the dense matter density should be substantially higher than the Planck density, thereby necessitating a ultra-high-density state for the dark matter as well.  We contend that this level of darkness and matter density is highly probable in the early universe, thereby setting the stage for this matter-matter model to be a compelling explanation for the existence of dark matter and matter.  To investigate the implications of this model on the cosmic and sub-cosmic scales, we utilize a modified $\Lambda$CDM model, which predicts a significant increase in the number of small dark matter halos, as well as an elevated density of dark matter in the solar neighborhood, thereby facilitating the occurrence of ultra-high-density events in the solar system.  We argue that this matter-matter scenario can be distinguished from the standard cold dark matter model by the frequency of ultra-high-density events in the solar system, with a predicted occurrence rate of approximately once every $10^4$ years, with the most recent event having occurred in $2001 AD$, when the neutron star PSR J1719-1438b was formed.

learning algorithm can selectively query a label
  oracle to obtain the labels for certain inputs.  Unlike traditional supervised learning,
  where the training data is generated according to the distribution of inputs alone, in
  supervised classification the label oracle typically provides the labels without any
  additional constraints or limitations.  Taking full advantage of this, we propose a new
  setting called Constrained Query Learning (CQL), where the oracle is limited in how the
  labels can be obtained.  Specifically, we introduce two constrained models: Lazy-Oracle
  (LO) and Noisy-Oracle (NO).  LO allows a single measurement of a Hermitian matrix whose
  elements are derived from the training data, whereas NO allows a noisy version of this
  measurement.  As a result, CQL represents a more data-efficient framework for training
  neural network classifiers compared to standard supervised learning.  To bridge the
  theoretical-practical gap, we develop gradient-based Constrained Supervised Learning
  (cURL) algorithms tailored to LO and NO that allow for gradient calculation and thus
  enable the use of conventional learning techniques like stochastic gradient descent.  We
  evaluate our methods through numerical experiments on multiple datasets, showing that
  cURL achieves the same level of accuracy as conventional supervised learning while
  requiring a significantly smaller number of labeled data points.

chemical systems is often
  characterized by complex patterns that emerge from underlying spatial or
  temporal structures.  This phenomenon can be effectively described by a
  hierarchical description of systems, utilizing concepts from geometry,
  statistical mechanics and dynamical systems theory.  Geometry provides the
  language to describe these patterns, while statistical mechanics and dynamical
  systems theory enable the prediction of patterns' behavior.  Recent research has
  focused on the application of hierarchical structures to understanding the
  state of systems, with promising results achieved in the study of geometric
  phases, multi-stability, topological defects, and more complex features.  This
  article provides an in-depth exploration of hierarchical structures in systems,
  covering the topics of geometric phases, multistability, topological defects,
  cohomology holes, and heteroclinic networks.  It examines how these topics are
  interconnected and explores their applications to real-world systems.  While
  numerous studies have explored individual topics in isolation, this review is
  among the first to investigate their interconnections and common underlying
  principles, offering insights for further research in this field.

The photoluminescence decay time was found to depend significantly on the thickness of the breakdown layer, particularly when it was less than a certain characteristic length, which is referred to as the tunneling distance. By analyzing the data, we calculated the tunneling distance to be approximately 2.5 nm. Time-resolved photoluminescence measurements revealed that when the superlattice barrier was smaller than the tunneling distance, electron and hole motion became decoupled, resulting in two distinct photoluminescence decay times. Conversely, when the barrier was larger, electrons and holes remained coupled, yielding a decay time equivalent to that of a standard GaAs quantum well. To gain further insights into carrier dynamics within these superlattices, we conducted terahertz spectroscopy measurements and modeled the results to determine key parameters such as drift velocity and carrier diffusion coefficients. Notably, we found that high carrier concentrations lead to a significant increase in the diffusion coefficient, particularly at concentrations exceeding $10^{11}$ cm$^{-2}$, which corresponds to a carrier density projected onto the interface plane.

We leverage the Na I D absorption lines in the spectra of starburst galaxies to estimate sodium concentrations as functions of galactic radial distance.  We analyze 113 absorption-line spectra from 10 starburst galaxies, obtaining sodium gradients of approximately $0.04$ dex/kpc for radial distances up to 2-3 times the optical diameter.  We find that this sodium gradient is steeper than expected from the Milky Way, likely due to higher sodium diffusion caused by increased gas content in the outer regions of these galaxies.  We compare our sodium gradient to those expected from metallicity gradients derived from various metal absorption lines in the spectra of these same galaxies.  We find that aluminum and magnesium gradients are significantly weaker than sodium, while iron gradient is comparable to sodium.  We conclude that sodium is a volatile metal that forms compounds with low condensation temperatures, which easily evaporate in the gaseous phase, and that these properties make sodium an ideal case study to understand the distribution of volatile metals in galaxies.

The underlying assumption is that the system's underlying physics can be represented by a set of uncertain but learnable equations.  The proposed approach involves using a Bayesian Gaussian process model to approximate these equations and then applying an approximate policy gradient learning method to develop control strategies based on this model.  The method is then refined using Bayesian model averaging to incorporate multiple model realizations and prevent overfitting.  The results of the refined strategy are then used to improve the accuracy of the control policies.  The method is particularly suited to scenarios where there is a need to balance exploration and exploitation in the face of limited training data.  The thesis includes a thorough examination of the performance of the method through numerical simulations and a collaborative experiment with the Fluid Dynamos facility. The experiment involved training and then applying the control strategy to control the onset of a Rayleigh-B\'enard convection in a laboratory setting. The results of the experiment showed that the method successfully achieved the desired level of flow suppression, despite the presence of experimental noise and a limited amount of data for refinement. The method's performance was measured in terms of a Gaussian process utility model and the results showed that the method successfully balanced exploration and exploitation in the face of limited training data.

We establish that the probability of visiting the root of such a tree follows a power law, which then allows us to extend previous findings regarding Sierpinski trees to a broader category of binary trees.  We prove that the probability of remaining in any particular subtree of a finite degree tree converges to a non-zero value as we consider deeper and more complex structures.  This convergence implies that digits in a tree's depth do not adhere to Benford's law, a result that holds for a broader class of trees including those where the power law exponent equals the reciprocal of the logarithm of the golden ratio.  However, we also demonstrate that a probability measure defined by an infinite product of a decreasing sequence within a specific range yields the observed values at the root of certain trees.  Consequently, these values can be determined from the observed values at the root, a finding that holds for a broader class of trees where the power law exponent is irrational.  This relationship can be expressed as a product formula, a result that has significant implications for understanding the values at the root of these tree structures.

high bandwidth and low latency connectivity is device-to-device (D2D) communication, in which nearby application devices transmit and communicate directly with each other. Concurrent algorithms that utilize comparison-based operations on ticket values present another complication, as these algorithms depend on both the relative ordering and specific numerical values of these comparisons.  In this research, we introduce a innovative specification method based on the use of concurrent data structure abstractions known as concurrent insertion sort lists (CISLs).  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by creating a specification for the renowned "fifo" ticket queue algorithm, also called "first-come, first-served."  Furthermore, we develop a CISL data structure and incorporate it into our "fifo" algorithm, thereby facilitating analysis of the data structure's properties to simplify the verification of the algorithm's correctness.  Our findings are significant as they establish that a ticket queue can be accurately represented by a CISL that provides sequentially consistent read access, multiple write operations, and the ability to determine when reads and writes occur in a sequentially consistent order.  This research contributes to the broader field of concurrent programming by providing a powerful tool for reasoning about complex algorithms and by showcasing the effectiveness of abstracting data structures in this domain.

Linguistic theories proposing underlying sequential representations, such as Linear Context-Sensitive Grammar, Chomsky's Phrase Structure Grammar, and Tree-Adjoining Grammar, all rely on diagrams that visually depict the relationships between language elements.  These diagrams, in turn, serve as a foundation for developing parsing algorithms designed to automatically analyze and interpret language structures. This paper delves into the connection between sequential language capabilities and the ability to understand and manipulate language structures, resulting in underlying diagrams that adhere to specific constraints. field of neural process-based methods, which enable a form of learning that involves generalizing over sequences of data. However, a major limitation of these approaches is their reliance on N-to-N mapping, which can be inefficient when dealing with specific tasks that involve a single output. This research introduces a neural process-based method known as Neural Higher-Order Regeneration (NHOR), which incorporates higher-order regression (HOR) into the process. The NHOR method enables the creation of a sequence encoder that generates a latent representation, which is then used to facilitate the reconstruction of both the preceding sequences and the final target. The consequences of dual reconstruction losses result in a decoder that is more sensitive to the underlying data distribution, leading to the development of a N-to-1 mapping function. The efficacy of the proposed NHOR method was validated through a set of synthetic and real-world datasets, showing improved performance over existing neural process-based methods in terms of accuracy and sample efficiency.

and heterostructures is heavily influenced by exciton localization. 
The exciton's internal structure, comprising an electron and a hole within an exciton wavefunction, plays a crucial role in determining this localization process. 
However, most existing studies focus solely on the exciton's overall behavior and do not address its internal dynamics. 
In this work, we develop a four-particle maximally coupled basis that accounts 
at an accurate level for both both the exciton's internal and center-of-mass 
motion within the effective mass approximation framework. 
This approach enables a precise calculation of exciton polarization as a 
function of its internal and external momenta, providing valuable insights 
into the exciton's spectral characteristics, particularly in strained and 
inhomogeneous structures. 
We demonstrate this method's effectiveness by analyzing the polarization 
dependence of Stokes shift and studying the momentum-resolved exciton 
spectra in strained quantum wells. 
Furthermore, our maxically coupled basis offers a comprehensive understanding 
of the interaction between the exciton's internal and external motion.

the Prisoner's Dilemma framework, which is at the heart of many public-good scenarios and has significant implications for societal issues such as pollution and resource depletion.  The Prisoner's Dilemma framework is an essential tool for researchers to employ when investigating the intricacies of human decision-making in various contexts, including economics, psychology, neuroscience, and evolutionary biology.  In this study, we investigate the impact of varying monetary amounts on human behavior within a Prisoner's Dilemma framework, utilizing data from multiple experiments where participants made decisions involving different stake levels.  Our empirical analysis reveals that increasing the monetary value of decisions leads to a greater tendency towards cooperation, likely due to the amplification of intrinsic motivations.  Moreover, our results indicate that the relationship between cooperation and stake size follows a nonlinear pattern, as opposed to a linear correlation, and this insight holds relevance for real-world situations involving decisions with diverse cost-benefit ratios.

has recently gained significant interest, 
  reflecting the belief that evolutionary histories of species undergo various 
  rearrangements over time.  In this research, we explore the concept of finding 
  a persistent phylogeny by comparing genomic genomes across different time 
  periods.  To achieve this, we define the problem of Persistent Phylogeny as 
  follows: given genomic genomes at two time points and corresponding data on 
  how genomes transform between these points via signed reversals, our goal is to 
  determine whether a consistent phylogenetic history exists that aligns with 
  this data.  In our analysis, we prove that it takes a polynomial amount of 
  computation to verify if a given history satisfies the requirements, but we 
  also show that finding such histories is dramatically more complex, requiring 
  double exponential computation to confirm.  Furthermore, we discover that 
  removing even a single reversal from any given hard instance results in a problem 
  that can be solved with relatively extensive, though still super-polynomial, 
  computation - specifically, 40 iterations of the FETTER algorithm provide a 
  definitive answer.

learning in autonomous driving has been accompanied by a growing interest in increasing model interpretability.  This study proposes a novel approach called Joint Feature Selection and Representation Learning (JFSRL), an iterative algorithm that leverages sparse optimization and deep learning to identify the most crucial visual elements in autonomous vehicles' reactions to complex traffic situations.  JFSRL modifies a traffic scene representation by incorporating a compact visual feature set, thereby enhancing the interpretability of decision-making processes in driving models.  By employing JFSRL, we discovered that only a small fraction of visual features, such as lane markings and road signs, are pivotal in predicting vehicle behavior in certain traffic scenarios, whereas other components like other vehicles and pedestrians play a minimal role.  JFSRL facilitates the interpretation of traffic scenarios and autonomous vehicle behavior in a unified framework, offering a clearer understanding of the relationship between visual features and simple semantic components.

has emerged as a pivotal tool in contemporary healthcare, facilitating the collection of vast amounts of patient data. Despite these advancements, NLP systems are prone to errors stemming from inherent limitations in current approaches and the complex nature of clinical language.  This paper presents a unified framework called Multi-View Clinical Representation Learning (MVCRL) that employs multiple data sources and modalities to enhance clinical NLP performance through a multi-view representation learning approach.  By integrating complementary information from electronic health records, clinical notes, and medical texts, MVCRL has shown significant improvements in various NLP tasks, including clinical document classification, relation extraction, and medical question answering.  Our research highlights the potential of MVCRL in developing more accurate and reliable NLP systems that can positively impact clinical care.

However, traditionally, finding the Koopman generator based on observations from a finite set of states is an intractable problem.  This research addresses stable Koopman invariant submanifolds and develops a finite-dimensional approximation of the generator based on a nonlinear attractor's trajectory.  By leveraging the structure of the submanifolds, we derive a method to obtain a finite basis for each eigenfunction corresponding to each Koopman eigenvalue, which allows us to design a low-rank approximation of the generator.  This generator approximation supports a data-driven predictive control law capable of stabilizing systems to a given trajectory.  The predictive control law utilizes a finite basis of the eigenspace associated with Koopman eigenvalues located near the origin, which can be obtained through a trajectory-based observability operator analysis.  Notably, this research is among the first to address the challenge of finding a Koopman generator in a noncompact phase space.

The performance of a PID controller can be significantly improved through optimal tuning, but this is challenging due to the vast number of PID variants and the impracticality of conducting extensive experiments for tuning purposes. depth cameras offer a cost-effective solution for three-dimensional vision, yet their depth measurements are often compromised by noise, particularly at greater distances.  This issue stems from the random interference caused by scattered near-infrared light.  Traditional denoising methods fail to produce reliable results due to the varying noise levels in different image regions.  In this study, we introduce a novel approach to denoise ToF depth maps by first estimating the noise distribution through a distribution estimation network (DEN).  Subsequently, a joint reconstruction and denoising framework is established, leveraging the predicted noise distribution as regularization to guide the three-dimensional convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) in learning a precise noise distribution.  Extensive experiments on two publicly available ToF depth datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in denoising ToF depth maps.  Notably, our approach outperforms 12 state-of-the-art methods in terms of mean squared error (MSE) and mean intersection over union (MIoU) metrics.  The source code for this project is publicly accessible at https://github.com/1000xLab/3D-RED.

reciprocal propagation of light in a phonon-assisted process within a lithium niobate waveguide. By utilizing a nanocrystalline lithium niobate containing near-infrared pumping and infrared signal transmission, we demonstrate nonreciprocal differences in transmission intensity and phase. Specifically, we observe a 20 dB phase shift between co- and counter-propagating cases under optimal conditions. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the nonreciprocal behavior is primarily driven by angular momentum conservation, highlighting the process' unique properties. Notably, this phonon-assisted propagation differs from traditional magnetism-based nonreciprocal phenomena in that it does not require high Cr3+ ion concentrations, avoiding the associated drawbacks such as crystal opacity and inhomogeneous broadening.

However, a critical issue arises as these methods typically overlook the influence of treatment choices on future observations, leading to the development of decision problems that are not Markovian in nature. Specifically, we introduce the Counterfactual Sequential Memory-based Observer (CSMO) model, which incorporates the information from past observations and future observations into its structure. This model allows for the direct optimization of a counterfactual objective function, which can be trained using the iterative Counterfactual Factual Optimization (CFO) algorithm. Ultimately, this study aims to facilitate the development of more effective and data-driven clinical decision-making systems.

every positive integer can be uniquely expressed as the sum of adjacent Fibonacci numbers, which are not the initial two Fibonacci numbers. neural network can efficiently identify and track non-rigid objects within a video, overcoming the limitations of previously achieved results in this area.  Object tracking with non-rigid targets is challenging due to their significant appearance changes and the use of deceptive background elements.  Conventional approaches that rely on crafting specific rules for each type of target are not scalable and often fail in the face of unforeseen scenarios.  Generic, off-the-shelf tracking algorithms are prone to being deceived by background elements and tend to converge to incorrect solutions.  Our proposed approach takes a learning-based strategy that consists of two stages.  Initially, we employ a encoder-decoder model to project a generic codebook onto a tailored, smooth, and discriminative feature space, achieving superior tracking results.  Specifically, our method utilizes a pre-trained two-stream neural network to extract features from video inputs, then employs the generic base to isolate the target, guided by the objective function that integrates two complementary goals.  The first goal aims to distinguish the target from its surroundings, while the second seeks to create a optimal solution within the target's neighborhood.  Our method's design confers several advantages, including robustness, efficiency, and compatibility with any pre-trained neural network.  Our code is available online at https://github.com/zhengcui/Codebook.  Our project was recognized as a runner-up in the MVTec Trackers Challenge 2019.

Our protocol, based on a lightweight consensus algorithm, is designed to prevent malicious actors from manipulating the routing tables and issuing incorrect forwarding rules.  Although the protocol incurs minimal computational costs, its implementation does come with increased memory usage for the routing tables.  Through extensive testing and simulations, our protocol has been shown to efficiently route the majority of traffic without requiring additional memory, outperforming the widely-used OpenFlow protocol in terms of routing efficiency.

In this research, we investigate the relationship between materials properties and magnetism in a range of nickelate compounds with different oxygenations and crystalline structures using first-principles calculations. set $V$ in a graph $G$ constitutes an $l$-path cover if $l$ vertex-disjoint paths from $V$ can cover $C$, denoted $\Pi(C, l)$.  The $l$-path cover number of graph $G$, denoted $\pi_{PC}(l)$, is the minimum size of subsets $C$ for which $\Pi(C, l)$ holds.  This study investigates $k$-path covers in graphs where $k$ has an even value.  We demonstrate that for any graph $G$, there exists an efficient algorithm running in polynomial time to determine whether $\pi_{PC}(k)$ is at most five times the minimum $k$-path cover subsets if $G$ can be covered with a circular interval graph structure. Additionally, we show that determining if $\pi_{PC}(k)$ is at most its circular interval graph thickness plus one for any $G$ is an NP-complete problem when $k$ is not restricted.

The non-uniform magnetic fields contain significant small-scale velocity and magnetic field components that interact and generate an average magnetic field over time.  The interaction between these components results in turbulent pressure and buoyancy forces that can be incorporated into stellar models in four different layers.  The model incorporates the effects of rotation and non-uniform magnetic fields, which cause angular velocity and field strength to vary across the star.  The interaction between these factors creates four distinct zones within the star where they do not intersect.  The star model converges when using the CCM method to solve this interaction.  The results show that turbulence accelerates the star's rotation, whereas the non-uniform magnetic fields have a slowing effect. In the context of a dark matter ULA model, we investigate how it can be reconciled with observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). In this framework, ULA is comprised of numerous independent, uncorrelated inflationary ULA fields, and is characterized by its overall amplitude, number of constituent fields, and their individual directions in field space. In this study, we calculate the initial conditions for the ULA field, and we determine the impact of the ULA's influence on the shape of CMB power spectra. In our analysis, we focus on scenarios in which the number of independent ULA fields is on the order of 100 to 1000, and we find that the model is constrained by Planck's observations of CMB anisotropies. In this study, we establish constraints on the model's parameter space, and we find that this space is largely consistent with regions that allow for the production of the universe's total matter content through the coherent collapse of multiple ULA fields.

The proposed structure, known as the spin filter, incorporates a transverse electric field to select the transverse spin state of a charge current without affecting the longitudinal spin state.  The study demonstrates that the difference between the total currents of parallel and antiparallel spin states along the longitudinal direction determines the transverse spin state.  The project also shows that the transverse spin state is controlled by the charge current strength, spin polarization, and the width of the armchair edge.  The study finds that the transverse spin state can be significantly amplified, up to $10^{-2}\hbar/e$ with an electric field of $0.1$ V/A, and that the spin filter coefficient, a measure of the transverse spin state's dependence on the charge current, reaches $10^{-1}$ under optimal conditions.  The project highlights the significant role of the spin Hall effect in achieving these results, and suggests that a transverse electric field can be used to generate and manipulate spin sources in graphene nanoribbons.

the outcome of sports games.  The team composition problem is typically addressed by making assumptions about the skill level and position of each individual player.  However, these approaches often overlook the complex interactions between teammates, which can either hinder or support one another.  In this study, we take a different approach by utilizing player–player connection weights to represent these interactions.  Using real-world data from NBA games, we collected connection weights based on the frequency of player interactions and utilized a deep learning model to extract meaningful patterns from this data. Our study paves the way for PCP systems to take player interactions into account in the future.

This work investigates the natural gradient within this context, defining the quantum Fisher information matrix and demonstrating that it can be explicitly computed for variations of parametric quantum circuits. This unnecessary information is known as paralinguistic, and it encompasses elements such as the speaker's tone, volume, speed, and emotional state. While speech recognition technology has made significant advancements, it inadvertently learns and utilizes paralinguistic features, often without our awareness. This is concerning, as these features can reveal sensitive information about individuals, which is not acceptable. To mitigate this issue, researchers are now focusing on developing more effective and data-efficient methods for paralinguistic feature extraction. This paper presents an in-depth exploration of paralinguistic feature learning, covering various aspects such as speaker and identity classification, accent classification, and providing a comprehensive overview of existing techniques and potential applications in the field.

1054 AD was extensively studied, several mysteries remain unsolved.  We propose a novel candidate for T2 type variable star in V1550 Cygni, located near the Crab Nebula.  Based on its spectral characteristics and periodic changes, this candidate exhibits a 11.51 months period, with variations of 0.09 magnitudes.  The V1550 Cygni candidate is located 1.24 light years from the Crab supernova, with a temperature of 5050 Kelvin and a magnitude of 10.3.  Its spectral features closely resemble those of the star observed in 1054 AD, suggesting it could have been visible to naked eye during the supernova event.  We suggest further studies, such as spectroscopic analysis of its companion star, to confirm this candidate as the T2 type variable star identified in 1054 AD.

there exist combinations of several complex scalar fields that form charge densities, exhibit richer dynamics and potential applications compared to single-field Q-balls.  We investigate the properties of multi-field Q-balls within a particular framework of Q-balls, where the potential is a collection of absolute values of complex polynomial terms and is relevant for models of inflation followed by Q-ball formation.  We demonstrate that these multi-field Q-balls can display remarkable behavior, such as expanding in size while mass remains constant or growing in mass while expanding in size.  We further explore whether these Q-balls can be stable in a universe dominated by relativistic particles and whether they can cross thresholds to create bubbles of a new, lighter vacuum.  We find that the expanding Q-ball dynamics are most beneficial for models in which the Q-ball enters the Q-ball-dominated era shortly after its formation.  We also examine how these dynamics are affected by interactions with the early universe, including the production of gravitational waves and non-Gaussianities in the CMB.

In this model, the scale factor evolves according to a power law, allowing for a steady state of the Hubble parameter and the torsion scalar within the context of the $f(T,B)$ gravity framework. , researchers employ
  techniques from algebraic topology, specifically persistent homology.  This work
  focuses on estimating the true distribution of multidimensional data from samples,
  particularly those samples that are relatively small.  Samples that are relatively
  small often occur in applications involving point clouds in biology and geography.
  A key challenge in estimating these samples is that conventional estimation
  techniques are computationally intensive and result in slow and inaccurate
  computations of algebraic topology features from samples.  This problem is
  compounded by the need to calculate topological features across multiple
  dimensions.  This work presents an estimation framework that is robust to samples
  that are relatively small from seven to ten dimensions.  The proposed approach
  involves two primary components: a multidimensional Poisson process that
  redefines the sample as; and a novel approximation of topological features that
  relies on solving systems of linear equations.  This proposed approach is
  found to yield precise results across samples of relative small size in
  dimensions seven to ten, outperforming existing methods and providing a robust

other prohibited items in images is a challenging task due to the limited availability of labeled training data.  Semi-supervised learning has emerged as a promising technique to address this issue by leveraging a small amount of labeled images and a large number of unlabeled images.  However, existing semi-supervised approaches often struggle to generalize well due to the reliance on restrictive assumptions and the potential negative impact of noisy unlabeled data.  In this work, we propose a new framework called Active Semi-supervised Learning (ASL) that combines semi-supervised learning with active learning to improve anomaly detection performance.  The ASL framework allows for the selective acquisition of informative images from unlabeled datasets in exchange for associated costs, thereby reducing the need for extensive labeling efforts.  We develop an efficient algorithm called Natural Policy Gradient (NPG) to optimize the ASL framework, which learns a policy to identify and request the most valuable images.  Our experimental results on public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the ASL approach in detecting anomalies such as knives and other prohibited items in images.  Furthermore, we believe that the ASL framework can be extended to other computer vision tasks and settings.

  Transformer an ideal choice for multi-task learning, but its inefficiency
  raises concerns about its practicality.  In this research, we question
  the benefits of the self-attention mechanism's global modeling capability
  and explore the possibility of enhancing multi-task Transformer
  performance by leveraging its redundant attention connections.  In its
  original design, self-attention connects all input tokens to all output
  tokens, creating $O(N^2)$ attention heads for processing $N$ input tokens.
  By utilizing only a subset of attention heads, we can both improve model
  efficiency and isolate specific task-related information.  Based on this
  concept, we developed the MAM-Transformer, a multi-task attention
  Transformer that incorporates the following key innovations:  a hard
  task-assignment mechanism that routes each token's output to a specific
  task;  an adaptive task-selection mechanism that dynamically chooses the
  most relevant token's output for each transformation;  and a sparse
  implementation that replaces the complex $O(N^2)$ self-attention with an
  efficient hard task-assignment module.  MAM-Transformer can be trained
  from scratch or adapted from pre-trained models through hard task
  assignment.  Experimental results on the IEMOCAP emotion classification
  dataset and the SST sentiment analysis show that MAM-Transformer achieves
  superior performance compared to existing multi-task attention models.

This paper introduces the StochAdjoint Operator Linearity Assessment (SOLA) method, a new way to evaluate and compare the performance of ensemble forecasting systems.  Using a maximum likelihood approach, SOLA assesses the linability of the forecasting system's responses to a set of perturbations.  This assessment provides a quantitative measure of how well the ensemble forecast system approximates a stochastic representation of its response to perturbations. Traditional approaches to deploying ML models on mobile devices involve transferring pre-trained models to the devices for local prediction, but this approach often results in high latency and excessive power consumption due to model downloading and forward propagation. In this research, we introduce a novel technique called Computation Offloading that transfers the computation associated with training the model to the cloud, shifting the model deployment focus to moving individual layers of the model between the cloud and mobile device during the training process. This method enables training deep models on mobile devices without downloading or running them locally, even when processing time is limited. Our offloading approach incorporates a new algorithm that determines the optimal placement of model layers, balancing the trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational overhead. Experimental evaluations show significant improvements in both accuracy and efficiency, with up to a 100% increase in achievable accuracy for the same computational cost, or a 10x reduction in computation for the same accuracy level, compared to traditional approaches of training and deploying models on mobile devices.

have achieved great success in various applications involving large-scale graphs, yet their training process is vulnerable to adversarial attacks due to embedded hierarchy.  Researchers have previously attempted to mitigate this vulnerability by designing robust aggregation functions and carefully pruning graph structures to identify and eliminate sensitive connections.  Nevertheless, these approaches either compromise the performance of encoded information by modifying aggregation functions or rely on heuristic-based strategies that may target susceptible layers or connections but not the actual adversarial nodes.  In this research, we propose a novel approach to generate adversarial nodes directly at the node level, thereby posing a significant challenge to existing defense methods.  Notably, some existing approaches are only capable of mitigating the influence of node features but fail to address the susceptibility of graph structures.  To tackle this issue, we propose a dual-enhanced neighbor learning framework that leverages node-level and structure-level features to enhance neighbor representations and filters out sensitive connections.  Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves superior performance in both primary and secondary tasks after the existence of adversarial nodes and existing defense methods are ineffective against it.

This paper delves into the implications of removing nonholonomic constraints from bipedal robots, specifically those with three legs, to understand the consequences of doing so. important topic in statistical mechanics.  A number of research papers have been published to investigate phase transition and critical phenomenon in various physical systems.  A common approach to studying phase transition is to examine the singularity of the free energy, which can be investigated through the partition function.  In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to analyzing phase transition and critical phenomenon by focusing on the eigenvalues of the transfer matrix.  Specifically, we demonstrate that the difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues of the transfer matrix is proportional to the susceptibility, providing valuable information about phase transition and critical phenomenon.  As practical applications of our proposed approach, we calculate susceptibility exponents for various models, including the one-dimensional Ising model with both short and long range interactions, and one and two dimensional Potts models.  Our results are in good agreement with existing literature, validating our proposed method.  Moreover, our approach offers a more intuitive understanding of phase transition and critical phenomenon by directly relating the susceptibility to the eigenvalues of the transfer matrix.  This could potentially lead to new insights and methodologies in this field of research.

Pareto distribution (GPD) are examined, focusing on the impact of shape parameter constraints, denoted as $\xi$, and prior distributions.  When $\xi$ is fixed at zero, the symmetry of GPD becomes equivalent to the log-logistic distribution.  Our research reveals that, in scenarios where $\xi$ is given a prior distribution centered around zero, the probability of symmetry can be elevated, even for datasets that indicate a somewhat skewed shape.  The efficacy of this approach in raising the probability of symmetry under various settings and shapes is analyzed and illustrated through numerical evaluations.  The problem of detecting symmetry within GPD is formulated as a hypothesis testing issue, comparing the null hypothesis of symmetry to an alternative where the shape parameter differs from zero.  The ability to accurately identify such differences and, consequently, detect asymmetries in extreme events, is assessed through the consideration of both frequentist and Bayesian frameworks, yielding findings that demonstrate a generally low power to identify actual asymmetries.

and Fast R-CNN have gained significant popularity in various detection tasks due to their high-precision and computational efficiency.  However, these methods are limited to handling only one type of detection problem.  To address this, we introduce a unified framework for region proposal, deep feature extraction, and classification/regression, designed to overcome the constraints of existing approaches.  To further enhance the method's performance, we propose introducing context and spatial information into the intermediate layer.  To address the issue of diverse detection targets having different contextual and spatial information requirements, we introduce an attention mechanism to dynamically regulate the importance of context and spatial features.  The proposed approach is called Star R-CNN, where the region proposal features, target features, and attention score interact with each other using the attention mechanism.  To optimize the network's efficiency, we employ a shared structure for bounding box regression and probability classification, along with a unique design of an overlapping star module that maximizes the use of shared components.  The attention mechanism was fine-tuned using a straightforward multi-task learning optimization technique.  Experimental results on the MS COCO dataset demonstrate that Star R-CNN achieves superior star structure efficiency and outstanding Star R-CNN performance compared to other detection methods.

We explore the possibility that a proposed feature, called goal alignment, can measure the degree of overlap between actions and descriptions. We present a generating set with exponential isoperimetric profile in a group that requires at least $n^2$ generators to represent any element of length up to $n$. responsible for how some

  still a significant debate regarding whether these formations result from 
  numerous small, interconnected cracks or a single major crack running from 
  the Earth's surface to its mantle. Our research utilizes numerical modeling 
  in order to investigate the propagation of magma-driven fractures in regions 
  with varying degrees of heterogeneity. Our models take into account the effects 
  of pre-existing weaknesses, such as faults, and how they interact with 
  ongoing fractures, as well as the impacts of varying degrees of rheological 
  homogeneity within the Earth's crust. Observations from seismic data and 
  geothermal measurements were used to inform our models, which we then compared 
  to satellite data on the ground's deformation. Our findings show that in 
  relatively uniform rheological settings, a single major crack tends to prevail,

  common. However, we found that the length of these fractures is overestimated 
  when using models with pre-existing weaknesses that are larger than what is 
  actually found in nature. Our study emphasizes the importance of detailed field

(ALP) is a hypothetical, very light, very weakly interacting, and very stable particle.  The interaction between ALPs and photons can be used to create a resonant conversion of photons into ALPs and vice versa in the presence of magnetic fields.  The goal of this work is to explore the potential for detecting ALPs using optical laser systems.  The proposed optical optical laser system can achieve extremely high sensitivity to ALP production or can even convert a fraction of the laser beam into a beam of invisible ALPs.  The system's performance is limited mainly by optical imperfections and can be significantly reduced through active feedback stabilization.  The generated ALP beam maintains its coherence and can travel vast distances without dispersion, unlike photons which scatter in magnetic fields.  The system's sensitivity is very high, with a lower bound of $1.0 \times 10^{-26} \text{ GeV}^{-1}$ for a generic ALP model over a wide mass range, and it can even generate an ALP flux of $1.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ cm}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$ at a distance of one light-year from the source.

Our study focuses on the problem of rumor detection on online forums, where users post questions and multiple answers. Unlike previous research, this problem differs in that the question and answer pairs are not pre-defined.
